name: Norðmǿrr
subtitle: Fylki of the Jarl
description: The people of the Norðmǿrr region, homeland of the Völsung, the royal house whose lands also reach Kattegat and Orkaldalr. To wear its crown is to accept a burden as much as an honour.

flokkr.name: Tryggr
flokkr.description: A sworn warband bound not by bloodline but by loyalty and brotherhood, in the direct service of the royal house of the Völsung.
flokkr.loreTitle: The Sworn Warband of Norðmǿrr Fylki
lore: In the northern lands, where the sea shaped the lives of men and the winter tested the strength of every household, warriors earned their standing through courage, loyalty, and the deeds by which they made their names known. In a world where rival chieftains pursued their own ambitions and alliances could shift with the fortunes of war, a man's worth was measured not only by the strength of his arm, but by the trust he inspired in those who stood beside him.
From these traditions emerged Tryggr Flokkr, a warband bound by loyalty, brotherhood, and a shared commitment to the path of the warrior.

Unlike the houses of the North, Tryggr Flokkr was not defined by bloodline or inheritance. Its identity rested upon the bonds between its warriors, their shared experiences, and the reputation they forged together. Men of different families could stand beneath its banner, united not by ancestry, but by their willingness to serve alongside one another and uphold the obligations they had accepted.

In time, Tryggr Flokkr entered the direct service of Norðmǿrr Fylki and the royal house of the Völsung. Through this allegiance, the warband assumed a position of particular trust, serving the crown and carrying out its commands wherever loyalty and martial strength were required.

Yet Tryggr Flokkr was never the royal house itself, nor was it merely an assembly of warriors gathered for a single campaign. It remained a distinct brotherhood, possessing its own identity, traditions, and standing. Its allegiance to Norðmǿrr did not erase its character; rather, its service to the crown became another measure by which its warriors were judged.

Under the authority of Norðmǿrr Fylki, the warband took part in campaigns, guarded royal interests, and accompanied military expeditions. Its warriors were expected to stand firm when called upon, maintain discipline in the face of adversity, and honour the trust placed in them. Their reputation rested upon their conduct as much as their victories, for strength without loyalty could bring glory to an individual, but it could not sustain a brotherhood.

The bonds within Tryggr Flokkr were therefore treated as obligations rather than empty words. A warrior's oath carried weight, and the trust between companions was something to be upheld through action. Those who served faithfully strengthened the standing of the warband, while those who abandoned their obligations risked bringing dishonour upon themselves and those who had placed their faith in them.

Beyond the battlefield, the North demanded resilience of its people. The sea provided both livelihood and passage, the land sustained the households that depended upon it, and the changing seasons reminded even the strongest warrior that survival required preparation, cooperation, and perseverance. These realities shaped the world in which Tryggr Flokkr operated, where warfare was only one part of a life governed by kinship, duty, and the struggle to endure.

As the years passed, the ambitions of northern warriors increasingly carried them beyond the familiar coasts. Trade, raiding, and military service offered opportunities to earn wealth and renown, while encounters with foreign rulers revealed possibilities that extended beyond the traditions of their homeland. For Tryggr Flokkr, such expeditions remained part of its service to Norðmǿrr Fylki, offering its warriors further opportunities to prove their worth.

Yet the consequences of these ventures could not always be foreseen. The choices made by warriors and their leaders could shape the fate of their companions, their descendants, and the traditions they carried with them.
For now, Tryggr Flokkr remained bound to its oath, serving Norðmǿrr Fylki and upholding the traditions that had forged its name.
But the world was changing, and the ambitions of men would not remain confined to the lands of their ancestors.
Eventually, one expedition would change the warband's future.

In the North, where the winters were harsh, the seas unforgiving, and the land demanded strength from those who called it home, survival was never the work of a single man. Families depended upon one another, chieftains gathered men beneath their banners, and the fate of entire settlements could rest upon the judgement of those who led them.

Yet strength alone could not unite the North. Rivalries endured, alliances fractured, and the authority of one chieftain rarely extended beyond the reach of his own influence. In a land where every household sought to preserve its standing, lasting unity was difficult to achieve.

From this world emerged Norðmǿrr Fylki, the people of the Norðmǿrr region, and from among them rose the Völsung, a royal house whose lands would come to reach Kattegat and Orkaldalr, and whose authority would come to represent something greater than the ambitions of a single family.

The foundations of Norðmǿrr were laid upon ancestry, obligation, and the recognition that those who ruled bore responsibilities beyond their own fortunes. The claim of its rulers rested upon the legacy of their bloodline, but their standing among the northern people depended upon their ability to preserve order, defend their lands, and lead their people through times of hardship and conflict.

To wear the crown was therefore to accept a burden as much as an honour. A ruler was expected to protect those under his authority, uphold the traditions of his ancestors, and ensure that the house he inherited would endure beyond his own lifetime. Royal blood might establish a claim, but it could not, by itself, guarantee the respect of the people or the stability of the realm.

Norðmǿrr Fylki consequently developed a tradition in which kingship and military strength were inseparable. The royal house maintained a disciplined hierarchy, with responsibilities distributed according to rank, trust, and duty. Those who held positions within its structure were expected to place the interests of the realm above personal ambition, understanding that the strength of the crown depended upon the conduct of those who served it.

This order distinguished Norðmǿrr from the lesser chieftains and competing households of the North. Where others might gather their strength only when conflict demanded it, the royal house sought continuity: a structure capable of preparing for war, maintaining alliances, and carrying the decisions of its rulers into action.

Nevertheless, Norðmǿrr remained a product of the North and its customs. The great hall was a place of counsel and hospitality, where agreements could be forged, disputes settled, and the deeds of ancestors remembered. Kinship established obligations between families, while reputation shaped the trust placed in those who held influence. A ruler who disregarded these traditions risked weakening the very foundations upon which his authority depended.
The crown therefore required more than obedience. It required recognition, and recognition had to be sustained through conduct.

In times of peace, the royal house was responsible for preserving the bonds that held its people together. Through alliances, negotiations, and the settlement of disputes, Norðmǿrr sought to prevent rivalries from consuming the strength of the realm. Its rulers were expected to exercise judgement, reward loyalty, and ensure that the interests of the kingdom were not sacrificed to the ambitions of individual households.

In times of war, these responsibilities became more immediate. The crown was expected to provide direction, gather the strength of the realm, and ensure that its people were prepared to defend their homes, their families, and their inheritance. Victory brought honour to the house, but defeat demanded accountability, for the consequences of a ruler's decisions rarely fell upon the ruler alone.

Yet the strength of Norðmǿrr did not rest upon its warriors alone. Its endurance depended upon the households that sustained the realm, the families that preserved its lineage, and the alliances that allowed its influence to extend throughout the North. The land provided sustenance, the sea offered both livelihood and passage, and the labour of generations ensured that the royal house possessed something worth defending.

For generations, Norðmǿrr looked towards the preservation of its legacy. Each ruler inherited not only the authority of those who came before, but also their unfinished obligations, their alliances, and the consequences of their decisions. The deeds of one generation could strengthen the next, just as the failures of a single ruler could leave burdens that endured long after his death.
Such was the nature of Norðmǿrr Fylki: a people bound to their ancestry and their land, loyal to their royal house, and ever mindful of the generations yet to come.

Beyond its homeland, the wider world continued to change. Trade brought new wealth, rival powers rose and fell, and the ambitions of northern rulers carried their attention towards possibilities beyond familiar territories. Norðmǿrr, like every enduring power, would eventually have to decide how it would face a world that did not stand still.

For now, however, the royal house remained rooted in the traditions that had shaped it. Its duty was to preserve the realm, uphold the authority of its crown, and ensure that the name of Norðmǿrr would endure.

For a dynasty is not measured by the years of a single reign, nor solely by the victories won beneath its banner, but by what remains when its rulers have passed and another generation inherits their burden.
The crown may pass from one generation to the next, but the duty of Norðmǿrr endures.

name: Orkaldalr
description: When the line breaks, it is the Orkaldalr Fylki that is dispatched to the faltering front. We run towards the danger, never away from it.
lore: Thanks to our advanced teamplay and experience in the game, we thrive in chaotic and dire environments where many casual players would fall. As a relatively small unit we have great mobility and autonomy on the battlefield, so we are the ones who choose the field of battle we fight on, not the enemy.

Whether you are a long-term veteran or a new player, you will learn something from our training, as we never shy away from improvement: it is our ultimate goal. Bearing our colors means you also bear our pride and will, so not everyone is trusted with membership. If you truly want to join the elite brotherhood, show courage and the will to get better. Once we see that in you, we will be the ones to reach out with an invitation.
